lab_title: Apparent Retrograde Motion: Solving the Martian Puzzle
top_level_objectives: Observe and define apparent retrograde motion from an Earth-bound perspective.
Understand the historical geocentric (epicycle) explanation for retrograde motion.
Explain retrograde motion as an optical illusion caused by Earth overtaking slower outer planets in a heliocentric model.
Analyze how a planet's distance from the Sun affects the size and frequency of its apparent retrograde loop.

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the phenomenon of retrograde motion exactly as ancient astronomers observed it from Earth.
key_visuals: A night sky dome featuring recognizable zodiac constellations.
Mars appearing as a distinct, bright reddish point of light against the stars.
A visible path trail that traces Mars's movement over time.
student_actions: Activate a time-lapse feature to fast-forward through several months of observation.
Observe Mars moving eastward, slowing down, looping westward (retrograde), and then resuming its eastward journey.
Mark the start and end dates of the retrograde loop on a virtual calendar.

scenes.brief_purpose: Explore the historical geocentric model and how it attempted to explain the retrograde loop using epicycles.
key_visuals: A 3D geocentric model with Earth at the center.
Mars attached to a small rotating wheel (epicycle) which is in turn attached to a larger orbit (deferent) around Earth.
A projected sightline showing how this physical loop creates the apparent motion in the sky.
student_actions: Manually rotate the deferent and epicycle to see how the combined circular motions produce a physical loop-the-loop.
Toggle the line-of-sight view to match the physical model's output with the observation from Scene 1.

scenes.brief_purpose: Reveal the true heliocentric structure of the solar system to set up the modern explanation.
key_visuals: A top-down view of the inner solar system with the Sun at the center.
Earth and Mars placed on their respective concentric orbits.
Orbital trails indicating the direction and relative speed of both planets.
student_actions: Start the orbital simulation to observe that Earth moves faster on its inner track than Mars does on its outer track.
Pause the simulation at the exact moment Earth pulls even with Mars (opposition).

scenes.brief_purpose: Connect the top-down heliocentric model to the Earth-bound observation by visualizing the line of sight.
key_visuals: The heliocentric model combined with a distant celestial sphere (background stars).
A bright, interactive line of sight extending from Earth, passing through Mars, and projecting onto the distant stars.
student_actions: Scrub time forward and backward through the 'overtaking' phase.
Watch the projected endpoint of the line of sight reverse direction on the star sphere precisely when Earth passes Mars on the inside track.
Toggle a split-screen view to simultaneously see the top-down perspective and the Earth-night-sky perspective.

scenes.brief_purpose: Solidify the relative motion concept using a familiar, everyday analogy.
key_visuals: A simplified highway or racing track with two cars.
The student's perspective placed inside the faster, inner car.
A slower car in the outer lane, with distant mountains or signs in the background.
student_actions: Drive the inner car past the slower outer car.
Observe how the slower car appears to drift backward relative to the distant background mountains, mimicking the planetary retrograde effect.

scenes.brief_purpose: Compare the retrograde motion of Mars to that of more distant planets to show the effect of distance on the optical illusion.
key_visuals: A zoomed-out heliocentric model that now includes the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.
Simultaneous line-of-sight projections for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn mapped onto the celestial sphere.
student_actions: Run the solar system simulation over a multi-year period.
Measure and compare the apparent width of the retrograde loops for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Conclude that the farther a planet is from Earth, the smaller and less dramatic its apparent retrograde loop becomes due to reduced parallax.
